<explanation>
Below is a detailed explanation for drawing an accurate system design diagram for Chisel, tailored to its specific purpose and structure.

1. Project Overview and Purpose:
   • Chisel is a tunneling tool that creates secure TCP/UDP tunnels over HTTP using SSH for encryption and authentication.
   • It is distributed as a single executable that contains both client and server capabilities.
   • The README emphasizes features such as encrypted and authenticated connections, reverse tunneling, SOCKS5 support, and additional proxy assistance. 

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   • Top-level directories include:
       - client: Contains client-side logic (client.go, client_connect.go, client_test.go)
       - server: Contains server-side logic (server.go, server_handler.go, server_listen.go)
       - share: Holds shared packages and utilities. Subdirectories here include:
           ▪ ccrypto: Cryptography routines (key generation, deterministic randomness, key helpers)
           ▪ cio: IO utilities like logging, pipe management, stdio connections (important for SSH and ProxyCommand)
           ▪ cnet: Networking utilities for handling TCP/UDP connections, WebSockets, HTTP server helpers, and connection stats
           ▪ cos: Common functions including pprof and signal handling
           ▪ settings: Handles configuration from environments, files, and remote settings (also contains authentication setup)
           ▪ tunnel: Contains tunnel logic (tunnel creation, both input and output handling, including UDP and SSH tunnels)
       - test: Contains benchmarks and end-to-end tests, showing that performance and network interactions are important.
       - example: Provides example configuration files (e.g., users.json, Flyfile, fly.toml) that may also be highlighted.

3. Main Components to Represent in the Diagram:
   a. Client Component:
       - Represented by the “client” directory and its related files.
       - Responsible for initiating connections to the server, maintaining tunnels, and handling local port forwarding, reverse tunnels, and SOCKS connections.
       - Uses shared libraries for network connections (cnet), tunnel management (tunnel), and cryptography (ccrypto).

   b. Server Component:
       - Represented by the “server” directory.
       - Listens for incoming connections, establishes tunnels, and manages HTTP and SSH-handled traffic.
       - Implements authentication (via settings and users files) and also supports reverse proxy and SOCKS5 modes.
       - Uses shared libraries similar to the client for core networking and cryptographic functions.

   c. Shared Libraries/Modules:
       - “share” acts as the library of common functions, covering:
            • Encryption & key management (ccrypto)
            • I/O handling and logging (cio)
            • Network connections and WebSocket support (cnet)
            • Signal handling and common utilities (cos)
            • Tunnel setup and management (tunnel)
            • Configuration and settings management (settings)
       - These should be depicted as “supporting modules” that both client and server rely on.

   d. External Interfaces and Flows:
       - Indicate how the client connects to the server over HTTP/HTTPS and how the tunnel transport uses SSH under the hood.
       - Draw connections for user-initiated commands (CLI) that run the client or server.
       - External networks: firewalls, destination endpoints (e.g., reverse proxy target, SOCKS5 connections), and, optionally, integration with Docker deployments (as hinted by .github and Dockerfile).

4. Relationships and Interactions:
   • Draw directional arrows from the client to the server to show connection flow.
   • Within both components, include internal flows such as:
         - From client: CLI → tunnel configuration → network connection setup → encrypted SSH handshake.
         - From server: Incoming network requests → authentication (using users.json or inline --auth) → session management → tunnel routing.
   • Show bidirectional communication for reverse tunneling (server listening and client proxying connections).

5. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Single-executable design that encapsulates both client and server logic.
   • A modular approach (separation of concerns) is evident in the distribution of common functionality into the “share” directory.
   • Use of Go interfaces and dependency injection (common in Go projects) to facilitate testing (see extensive testing directories) and clear responsibilities.
   • Emphasis on performance and concurrency (supported by benchmark tests and the use of efficient Go libraries).

6. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Go Programming Language (with its standard libraries for networking, crypto, etc.)
   • SSH protocol (for encryption and authentication)
   • HTTP/HTTPS for tunnel transport
   • WebSockets as an alternative connection mechanism when traversing proxies
   • Docker (as indicated by Dockerfile and CI workflows)
   • GitHub Actions (CI workflows under .github directory) and dependabot, which are part of the overall project maintenance but less critical on the architecture diagram.

7. Guidelines for the Diagram’s Layout:
   - Use distinct shapes or colors to differentiate major components:
         • Rectangles for core modules (Client, Server, Shared Modules).
         • Ovals for external entities (end-users, external endpoints, proxies, firewalls).
   - Clearly label each module/component.
   - Use directional arrows to indicate:
         • Data flow (e.g., command inputs, tunnel initiation, encrypted data paths).
         • Dependencies between the client/server components and underlying shared libraries.
   - If possible, include annotations to show the layered architecture:
         Layer 1: User/CLI interface.
         Layer 2: Client/Server Application Logic.
         Layer 3: Shared libraries (cryptography, network I/O, tunnel handling).
         Layer 4: External network/infrastructure (firewalls, proxies, target hosts).

8. Tailoring to Chisel’s Specific Architecture:
   - Emphasize the dual-role nature (client and server modes) within the diagram. You may split the diagram into two main sections – one for client operations and one for server operations – while showing their interactions via the network.
   - For each section, include the internal modules (for example, under “client” note modules dealing with connection establishment, tunneling, and reconnection logic as indicated by exponential backoff handling).
   - Under the “server” section, highlight authentication processing (keyfile, --auth/--authfile) and the integration with reverse proxy and SOCKS5 services.
   - Include a “shared” block which is used by both, making clear that aspects like encryption (with ECDSA keys) and configuration handling are common.
   
9. Final Instructions for the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Begin by outlining the high-level architecture: separate boxes for Client, Server, and Shared Modules.
   • Draw directional arrows to illustrate the flow of connection establishment, authentication, and data tunneling between client and server components.
   • Clearly label each component along with its key responsibilities. For example:
         - “Client: Manages tunnel requests, reconnections, and local port forwarding.”
         - “Server: Accepts connections, verifies authentication, and forwards traffic.”
         - “Shared Modules: Handle encryption (ccrypto), networking (cnet), IO (cio), tunnel management (tunnel), and configuration (settings).”
   • Use a color scheme or different shapes to help distinguish between the client, server, and library layers, and ensure that all external dependencies (e.g., proxies, external endpoints) are also represented.
   • Finally, include notes or annotations indicating that the design diagram should be as detailed as possible – breaking the project into its component layers to reflect the full end-to-end tunnel architecture implemented by Chisel.

Following these guidelines will result in a comprehensive and accurate system design diagram that captures the essential architectural elements and interactions inherent in the Chisel project.
</explanation>
